title: Anisotropic magneto-elastic coupling in the quasi-2D Ising magnet Li$_2$FeSiO$_4$ and thermodynamic signature of low-energy orbital excitations
authors: Waldemar Hergett, Kevin Ackermann, Sven Spachmann, Martin Jonak, Mahmoud Abdel-Hafiez, Hend Shahed, Michael Merz, Maurits W. Haverkort, Rüdiger Klingeler
abstract: The relevance of spin, lattice and orbital degrees of freedom in the quasi-2D Ising-like magnet Li$_2$FeSiO$_4$ is demonstrated by thermal expansion and specific heat measurements supported by numerical studies. By means of thermodynamic and Grüneisen analysis, we separate the orbital signatures and quantify the energy gap and its pressure dependence from the experimental data as $Δ\sim 300 - 350$ K and $\partial \ln Δ/\partial p_{\rm c} \approx -4.6$ %/GPa). Both values excellently agree with the theoretical DFT predictions. The thermal expansion anomalies associated with the onset of long-range magnetic order imply significant magneto-elastic coupling and are used to determine the anisotropic uniaxial strain dependencies of $T_{\rm N}$. They are dominated by the in-plane (i.e., $c$ axis) response $(\partial \ln{ T_{\rm N}} )/\partial p_{\rm c} \simeq 15$ %/GPa while the (negative) $a$ axis and (positive) out-of-plane ($b$ axis) pressure dependencies are much smaller. Short-range magnetic order extends well above $T_{\rm N}$ but is not driven by the same energy scale as $T_{\rm N}$ as evidenced by the observation of non-monotonic in-plane distortion, sign-change of the Grüneisen parameter, and failure of Grüneisen scaling.
summary: This work thoroughly investigates the coupled spin, lattice, and orbital physics in the magnet Li2FeSiO4. By combining dilatometry and specific heat measurements with DFT theory, the authors quantify the orbital energy gap and precisely map the anisotropic magneto-elastic coupling responsible for the magnetic transition. The findings provide a detailed picture of how electronic structure dictates macroscopic material properties under strain and temperature.
main_problem: The study investigates the complex interplay between spin, lattice, and orbital degrees of freedom in the quasi-2D Ising magnet Li2FeSiO4.
main_result: The research successfully quantifies the orbital energy gap ($\Delta \sim 300-350$ K) and determines the anisotropic magneto-elastic coupling constants governing the magnetic transition temperature ($T_N$).
method: The authors combine extensive experimental measurements (thermal expansion, specific heat) with theoretical DFT calculations and thermodynamic analysis (Grüneisen analysis) to separate contributions.
model_or_system: The physical system is the quasi-2D Ising-like magnet Li2FeSiO4, whose magnetic and structural properties are analyzed relative to its non-magnetic analog, Li2ZnSiO4.
key_observables: Thermal expansion coefficients ($\alpha_i$), specific heat components ($c_{	ext{mag}}, c_{	ext{orb}}, c_{	ext{ph}}$), orbital energy gap ($\Delta$), and critical exponents ($	ilde{\alpha}_{cp}$).
important_parameters: Magnetic ordering temperature ($T_N \approx 17.2 	ext{ K}$), pressure dependence of $\Delta$ ($\partial \ln \Delta / \partial p \approx -4.6 \%/	ext{GPa}$), and anisotropic strain dependencies of $T_N$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on separating phonon, magnetic, and orbital contributions to the specific heat, favoring Debye scaling over purely phenomenological approaches.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate relative length changes along $a, b, c$ axes, the decomposition of non-phonon specific heat into Schottky and magnetic parts, and the temperature dependence of various thermodynamic quantities.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first characterizing the anisotropic thermal expansion and magneto-elastic coupling at $T_N$, then decomposing the specific heat into phonon, magnetic, and orbital contributions, and finally using pressure and temperature dependence analyses to quantify the orbital gap and coupling constants.
why_interesting: The detailed separation of orbital excitations from magnetic and lattice contributions using thermodynamic analysis is highly relevant for understanding strongly correlated materials where multiple degrees of freedom interact.
